neighbours.label: legal-reasoning vocabulary about what a court decides: questions/findings of fact, the facts of an incident, the merits, a legal test, making out a case (not everyday 'fact' or 'test', not legal procedure)
fire: Whether the driver was negligent is a question of fact for the jury, not a question of law.
The tribunal dismissed the appeal without reaching the merits of the dispute.
The prosecution's evidence was not enough to make out a case of fraud.
The judges adopted a three-part test for deciding when a search is unreasonable.
The appellate court will not disturb findings of fact made by the trial judge.
Having disposed of the procedural objection, the court turned to the merits of the petition.
An expert was appointed to help the tribunal establish the facts of the collision.
The complaint must allege facts sufficient to make out each element of the offence.
quiet: The trial was postponed until March because the defence lawyer was ill.
The clerk stamped the documents and sent copies to both attorneys.
As a matter of fact, the restaurant had closed two weeks earlier.
The nurse ran a blood test and called with the results the next day.
The judge wore a black robe and entered the courtroom at nine o'clock.
The scholarship is awarded on merit to two students each year.
The law firm moved its offices to the tenth floor of a new tower.
The witness arrived late and was sworn in after the lunch break.

notes: Probing: 'facts of the incident' 0.82, 'merits of the claim' 0.71, 'two-part test' 0.59, 'questions of fact and law' 0.45, 'make out a prima facie case' 0.42; 'In fact', a math test and a lawyer filing a motion under 0.04. The + pole takes other court vocabulary (judgment, contempt, citations).
